relationships.description: The whole definition embeds the part definition as an owned constituent, such as a value object or line item, that has no meaning or identity outside the containing type.
relationships.evidence: A property of the containing definition uses '$ref: #/definitions/{part}' (or an array of it), and the part definition is referenced nowhere else and carries no identifier of its own.

relationships.description: The data type can only be validated, stored or interpreted correctly with a particular platform product, such as a database engine version or a JSON Schema validator runtime.
relationships.evidence: The schema uses a draft version, format or vendor keyword (e.g. a database-specific type annotation) that the named product's documentation or config declares support for, or the validation library is pinned in a dependency manifest.

relationships.description: Instances of the data type are persisted as records or documents in the collection, with the definition's properties corresponding to that container's columns or fields.
relationships.evidence: An ORM entity, migration or collection validator ($jsonSchema) declares the table or collection with fields matching the definition's properties, or a mapping annotation links the two by name.

relationships.description: The API schema is the wire representation of the domain data type, carrying the same structure, or a projection of it, in requests or responses.
relationships.evidence: The OpenAPI components/schemas entry is generated from, $refs, or field-for-field mirrors the JSON Schema definition, as shown by a codegen config or a shared schema file.

relationships.description: The definition is the formal data-level specification of the business concept, giving the business object's information a concrete structure and set of attributes.
relationships.evidence: The definition's title or description names the business object, and a domain glossary or data dictionary traces the business term to this '#/definitions/{name}' entry.

relationships.description: The code-level class, record or struct is the in-program form of the data type, holding exactly the state the definition describes.
relationships.evidence: The class is generated from the definition by a schema-to-code tool, or is annotated or validated against '#/definitions/{name}' with matching field names and types.

relationships.description: The definition points to the business process that creates or consumes its data, for example through a process identifier or a lifecycle-state enumeration, without depending on the process to be valid.
relationships.evidence: The definition's description, an x-extension or an enum documents the process or its stages by name, such as a status field whose values are the steps of the order fulfilment process.

relationships.description: One data type points to another by identifier or link, such as a foreign-key style ID, so the referenced type keeps its own independent lifecycle and is not embedded.
relationships.evidence: A property holds the other type's identifier, typed via '$ref: #/definitions/{other}/properties/id' or documented as an identifier of that type, rather than embedding the full object.

relationships.description: The definition names a threat in the threat model that its data is exposed to, such as injection through a free-text field or tampering with an identifier.
relationships.evidence: The definition's description or an x-threat extension cites the threat-model entry ID, or the threat-model document lists this definition as the affected asset.

relationships.description: Records of this data type must be kept for the policy's minimum period, held in the storage the policy specifies, and disposed of as the policy prescribes once that period ends.
relationships.evidence: An x-retention annotation on the definition names the policy, or the retention policy document lists this data type, with TTL or archival jobs configured to match.

relationships.description: The definition's structure complies with a stated restriction, such as a mandated data standard, field-length limit or jurisdictional data rule, and so keeps the design within the permitted solution space.
relationships.evidence: An ADR or requirements trace cites the constraint and the definition, and the schema's keywords (e.g. format, maxLength, mandated enum codes) implement the restriction.

relationships.description: The definition carries a sensitivity label and applies that tier's handling rules to its fields, such as marking fields for encryption or masking.
relationships.evidence: An x-classification or similar annotation on the definition names the tier, with field-level markers (e.g. x-encrypted, x-pii) matching the tier's obligations.

relationships.description: The definition provides the data structure, fields and validation rules that a verifiable requirement calls for, such as capturing a mandatory attribute or enforcing a value range.
relationships.evidence: A requirement trace matrix or the definition's x-requirement annotation links the requirement ID, and the schema's required, pattern or range keywords match the acceptance criteria.

relationships.description: The definition supplies the shared data contract the component uses to validate, construct and exchange the data it encapsulates.
relationships.evidence: The component's source imports or loads the schema file and validates payloads against '#/definitions/{name}', or generates its types from it at build time.

relationships.description: The definition specifies the payload structure carried by the event, so emitters and handlers agree on its contents.
relationships.evidence: An AsyncAPI document, event catalog or schema-registry subject binds the event's payload to the definition, or the publisher validates the event body against it.

relationships.description: The definition describes the input or output data that the function reads, transforms or produces.
relationships.evidence: The function's parameter or return type is generated from the definition, or its body validates input against '#/definitions/{name}'.

relationships.description: The definition provides the data shape of the operation's request body, response body or parameters.
relationships.evidence: The OpenAPI operation's requestBody or response content $refs a schema bundled or derived from this definition, or the route handler validates against it.

relationships.description: The subtype definition is a more specific variant of the parent type: it inherits all of the parent's properties and constraints and adds its own.
relationships.evidence: The subtype definition uses 'allOf' with '$ref: #/definitions/{parent}' plus additional properties, often with a discriminator value identifying the subtype.

notes: The three serves relationships to component, function and operation overlap with realizes→dataobject and maps-to→api.schema, which are the more precise links. Also, 'requires' RetentionPolicy is a poor fit: that policy covers security data such as audit logs rather than domain types. 'satisfies' DataClassification would read better as governed-by/constrained-by.
